newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Railtrack profits raise further steam.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Railtrack profits raise further steam.

text.p: British railways operator Railtrack Plc had to defend a sharp rise in profits in announcing its first set of annual results since privatisation on Thursday, rejecting renewed allegations of profiteering at the expense of investment.

Operating profits rose to 339 million pounds ($553.2 million) for the year to March 31, up from 296 million pounds last time, on turnover up 137 million pounds at 2.437 billion. The final dividend was increased 7.6 percent to 14.8p, making 22.1p for the full year, covered by earnings of 58.4 pence.
The company, which was sold off to investors for 1.93 billion pounds in May last year, said pre-tax profits rose 27 percent to 346 million pounds.

"I do not think we are making too much money," said chairman Sir Robert Horton. "I think we are being just about adequately rewarded for the capital, both in terms of intellectual capital and physical capital, that we are putting into the business," he told Reuters.

Horton said Railtrack had already helped cut passenger train delays across the network by 30 percent last year and he vowed to work with the train companies to get more passenger and freight traffic back on to the railways and off the roads.
"The tangible improvements in service which we promised are being delivered and we continue to pursue our ambition to create the world's best railway," he said in his results statement.

But the euphoria was shortlived. Railtrack's share price jumped 21-1/2 pence to 667 on the results, only to slip back to close at 658p after the industry's official regulator John Swift launched a fresh attack on Railtrack's investment performance.

Swift announced that in view of the results he was calling in Railtrack to review the level of performance bonuses it was getting from its customers, the train operators, and repeated his complaints that the company was lagging behind on its investment programme.
It still had a 400-million pounds backlog on spending on stations and a 277-million pound backlog on track and structure renewals, he said.

"These record profits show that Railtrack has funds available," he said in a statement. "They still have a long way to go before I can be satisfied that the long term health of the network is assured."

Horton reacted angrily, denying that Railtrack was dragging its feet, and noting that the firm was planning to spend 15.9 billion pounds on maintenance, renovation and new projects over the next decade, including one billion pounds on overhauling 2,500 stations.
"It is quite unreasonable to expect us to get up and modernise every single station in this country overnight. We are getting on with that as fast as we can," he told Reuters.
"Considering the extraordinary improvements that we have already achieved, perhaps looking back in five years time people will wonder what all this fuss was about."
Railtrack also rejected allegations by pressure group Save Our Railways that it was allowing the state of the network's track to deteriorate "to a dangerous extent."

Chief executive John Edmonds said the company spent 961 million pounds on infrastructure last year, up 29 percent on the previous year, and that it was 105 million pounds ahead of programme in its agreed investment plans.
"The idea that we are underinvesting is totally wrong," he told reporters.

Edmonds said poor track would lead to speed restrictions and consequent delays in train services. Instead the improvement in punctuality and reliability last year had been a dramatic 30 percent he said.
"If track were deteriorating in the way that our Save Our Railways friends are suggesting that result could not conceivably be achieved...We could not maintain punctuality."

He also rejected the suggestion that the debt reduction which Railtrack had enjoyed when it was privatised should make it liable to the new Labour government's proposed windfall tax on excess profits made by privatised utilities.
Edmonds said it would be "silly" for Railtrack to pay a windfall tax because the industry was still heavily subsidised by the government through the train operating companies.
Last year the 25 train operators paid Railtrack 2.12 billion pounds, almost its entire revenue.
"For the Treasury to impose a windfall tax on Railtrack when the Treasury itself funds the industry is a slightly circular and tortuous argument," he said.
"It doesn't make it impossible, it just makes it rather silly."($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
